newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton prices seen rising in India, Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton prices seen rising in India, Pakistan.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to rise in India and Pakistan on increased demand, dealers said on Thursday.
In India prices bounced back from lower levels in the local markets last week, dealers said.
"While mill buying remained low, increased purchases by the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI) dragged prices up from the recent lows," said one dealer.
Earlier the government allowed CCI to export 100,000 bales (170 kg each), triggering higher purchases by the corporation.
In spot deals, Bengal-deshi rose to 840/875 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) from 820/850 rupees while Punjab saw-ginned moved up by 40/60 rupees to 1,460/1,640 rupees per maund.
Gujarat Sankar-4 (long-staple) rose to 18,000/18,600 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) from 17,500/18,000.
"Eased pressure of new crop arrivals at the producing centres also helped market to bounce back," one broker said.
Lower prices and severely cold weather curtailed cotton arrivals at the producing centres, traders said.
"Market sentiment also turned firm during the week as government had allowed more export of 15,000 tonnes of cotton yarn," he said.
"Sentiment is turning firmer as traders were expecting more export quota for cotton and yarn in the coming days," said Manubhai Amersey, a leading dealer.
"Actually exporters from Pakistan had failed to honour shipments due to acute shortage and (therefore) European as well as American buyers are turning to India for cotton purchases," he added.
In Pakistan, prices rose on lower estimates of the 1996/97 (July-June) crop at 8.5 to 8.9 million 170-kg bales compared to a target of 10 million, dealer Shakoor Dada said.
The lower estimates, which triggered increased purchases by textile mills, raised the prices, Dada said.
Another factor for the rise was the shortage of good quality cotton, broker Adil Nasim said.
Analysts say dealers have to import about 500,000 bales of 480-lb each from Central Asia to feed the spinning industry on increased export commitments of yarn at a good price.
Traders had already imported 80,630 bales -- 35,522 by sea and 45,108 by land via Afghanistan -- by October 31 of the current fiscal year, which started in July, one dealer said.
High prices had kept cotton exporters away from the domestic markets, Adil Nasim said.
In the kerb market, the rate for NIAB-78 ranged between 2,432 and 2,440 rupees per maund (37.32 kg), Dada said.
